paragraphs: Linear algebra is the mathematics of lists of numbers and the tables that act on them. A list such as (4, 1) can stand for a place on a map or the push on a bridge, and a table of numbers can stretch, turn or flatten every such list on a plane at once. People study it because the same few ideas run through computer graphics, physics, statistics and machine learning, and because it is the standard way of reasoning about many numbers together.

The course has twenty lessons in five parts of four. Work with vectors covers coordinates, adding, dot products and directions of length 1. Build linear maps introduces matrices and what they do to the plane. Solve and describe turns to equations and the spaces they carve out. Measure the structure covers rank, determinants, projections and fitting a line to noisy measurements. Separate the directions ends with eigenvectors and the singular value decomposition.
Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards, so a question comes only once you have been shown what it needs.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a vector, add and scale vectors, and find a length or a dot product.
You'll be able to apply a matrix to a vector and say what it does to the plane.
You'll be able to solve a small system of equations by row reduction and say how many solutions it has.
You'll be able to find a determinant, a projection and a least-squares fit for small examples.
You'll be able to find the eigenvectors of a 2 × 2 matrix and read what a singular value decomposition reports.
prerequisites: You should be comfortable with signed arithmetic, simple equations and reading points on a coordinate graph.
